Ram Dass.bio: Ram Dass, born Richard Alpert, was an American spiritual teacher and former Harvard psychologist whose work with Timothy Leary on psychedelics made him a counterculture figure. After meeting guru Neem Karoli Baba in India in 1967, he took the name Ram Dass ('servant of God') and wrote the landmark book Be Here Now (1971). He spent the rest of his life teaching Eastern spirituality, compassion and conscious aging to Western audiences.

Deepak Chopra.bio: Deepak Chopra is an Indian-American author and alternative medicine advocate, trained as an endocrinologist, who became one of the best-known popularizers of Ayurveda and mind-body medicine. His books, including The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success (1994), have sold tens of millions of copies worldwide. He co-founded the Chopra Center for Wellbeing in California.

Sadhguru.role: Yogi and founder of the Isha Foundation
Sadhguru.bio: Sadhguru, born Jaggi Vasudev in Mysuru, India, is a yogi and mystic who founded the Isha Foundation in 1992, a non-profit offering yoga programs worldwide. His book Inner Engineering (2016) became an international bestseller. He is a frequent speaker at the United Nations, World Economic Forum and leading universities.

Sri Sri Ravi Shankar.role: Spiritual leader and founder of the Art of Living Foundation
Sri Sri Ravi Shankar.bio: Sri Sri Ravi Shankar is an Indian spiritual leader who founded the Art of Living Foundation in 1982, which teaches the Sudarshan Kriya breathing technique and stress-relief programs in more than 150 countries. He has been widely recognized for humanitarian and peace work, including mediation efforts in conflict zones. His teachings emphasize meditation, service and a stress-free, violence-free society.

Stephen Hawking.bio: Stephen Hawking was an English theoretical physicist and cosmologist who predicted that black holes emit radiation, now called Hawking radiation. Diagnosed with motor neurone disease at 21 and given a few years to live, he spent over five decades in a wheelchair communicating through a speech synthesizer. His book A Brief History of Time (1988) sold more than 10 million copies and made him the world's most famous scientist.

Richard Feynman.bio: Richard Feynman was an American theoretical physicist who shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on quantum electrodynamics. A member of the Manhattan Project as a young man, he later became famous for his bongo-playing, safecracking and irreverent memoir Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985). His Caltech lectures remain a classic of science teaching, and he famously exposed the O-ring failure behind the Challenger disaster.

Neil deGrasse Tyson.bio: Neil deGrasse Tyson is an American astrophysicist who has directed New York's Hayden Planetarium since 1996. He hosted the 2014 revival of Cosmos and the talk show StarTalk, bringing astronomy to mass audiences. His book Astrophysics for People in a Hurry (2017) was a long-running bestseller.

Bill Nye.bio: Bill Nye is an American science educator and mechanical engineer who hosted the award-winning children's show Bill Nye the Science Guy (1993-1998), which taught science to a generation of viewers. He later became CEO of the Planetary Society and a prominent voice on climate change. His Netflix series Bill Nye Saves the World (2017-2018) applied his signature style to adult audiences.

Jane Goodall.bio: Jane Goodall is an English primatologist who began studying wild chimpanzees at Gombe Stream National Park, Tanzania, in 1960, and overturned science's understanding of tool use and animal emotion. She founded the Jane Goodall Institute in 1977 and the youth program Roots & Shoots in 1991. Named a UN Messenger of Peace, she has spent decades campaigning for animal welfare and environmental protection.

David Attenborough.bio: Sir David Attenborough is an English broadcaster and natural historian whose landmark BBC series, beginning with Zoo Quest (1954) and including Life on Earth (1979) and Planet Earth (2006), defined the nature documentary. Over a career spanning more than 70 years, he has filmed wildlife on every continent. In later life he has become a leading voice on climate change and biodiversity loss, notably in A Life on Our Planet (2020).

Alexander Fleming.bio: Sir Alexander Fleming was a Scottish bacteriologist whose accidental discovery of penicillin in 1928, from a mould contaminating his culture plates at St Mary's Hospital, London, ushered in the antibiotic era. Developed into a drug by Florey and Chain, penicillin transformed medicine and saved hundreds of millions of lives. Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery.

B. F. Skinner.role: Psychologist and founder of radical behaviorism
B. F. Skinner.bio: Burrhus Frederic Skinner was an American psychologist who developed the theory of operant conditioning and invented the operant conditioning chamber, known as the 'Skinner box'. A Harvard professor for most of his career, he argued that behavior is shaped by its consequences of reinforcement and punishment. His books, including Walden Two (1948) and Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971), made him one of the most influential and controversial psychologists of the 20th century.

Ivan Pavlov.bio: Ivan Petrovich Pavlov was a Russian physiologist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his work on the digestive system. His experiments with dogs, which learned to salivate at the sound of a bell associated with food, revealed the conditioned reflex, a cornerstone of behavioral psychology known as classical conditioning or 'Pavlovian' learning. He ran a large research institute in St. Petersburg well into his eighties.

Jules Verne.role: Novelist and pioneer of science fiction
Jules Verne.bio: Jules Verne was a French novelist whose 'Extraordinary Voyages' series, including Journey to the Center of the Earth (1864), Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas (1870) and Around the World in Eighty Days (1872), made him a founding father of science fiction. Writing in Amiens, he imagined submarines, space travel and world travel long before they were practical. He remains one of the most translated authors in the world.

H. G. Wells.bio: Herbert George Wells was an English writer who pioneered science fiction with The Time Machine (1895), The Invisible Man (1897), The War of the Worlds (1898) and The First Men in the Moon (1901), imagining time travel, invasion and spaceflight decades ahead of reality. He was also a prolific social commentator whose Outline of History (1920) became a bestseller. Nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature four times, he is often called the father of science fiction.

F. Scott Fitzgerald.bio: Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was an American novelist whose masterpiece The Great Gatsby (1925) became the defining portrait of the Jazz Age and is now ranked among the greatest American novels. His other works include This Side of Paradise (1920) and Tender Is the Night (1934). He died in Hollywood at 44, believing himself a failure, shortly before Gatsby's posthumous canonization.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Rudyard Kipling.bio: Rudyard Kipling was an English poet and storyteller born in Bombay, India, whose works include The Jungle Book (1894), Kim (1901) and the poem 'If—' (1910), repeatedly voted among Britain's favourite poems. A journalist in India as a young man, he drew on the British Empire's landscapes and soldiers for his ballads and tales. In 1907 he became the first English-language writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature, and still its youngest recipient.

William Wordsworth.bio: William Wordsworth was an English poet who, with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, launched the Romantic movement with their joint Lyrical Ballads (1798), arguing for poetry in the language of common life. Living in the Lake District, he wrote beloved lyrics such as 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud' and the autobiographical epic The Prelude, published after his death. He served as Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death in 1850.

Christina Rossetti.bio: Christina Rossetti was an English poet of Italian descent, sister of the Pre-Raphaelite artist Dante Gabriel Rossetti, for whom she modelled. Her collection Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862) established her reputation, and her devotional verse and the carol 'In the Bleak Midwinter' kept her famous after her death. Long underrated, she is now regarded as one of the finest Victorian poets.

Sylvia Plath.bio: Sylvia Plath was an American poet and novelist best known for her novel The Bell Jar and the posthumous Ariel poems. Her intensely confessional writing explored identity, depression and the natural world. She was awarded a posthumous Pulitzer Prize for her Collected Poems in 1982.

Hafiz.bio: Khwaja Shams-ud-Din Muhammad, known as Hafiz of Shiraz, was a Persian lyric poet whose Divan is the most beloved poetry collection in Iran. His ghazals on love, wine and divine longing have been translated into many languages. His work later inspired Goethe's West-Eastern Divan.

Allama Iqbal.bio: Sir Muhammad Iqbal, known as Allama Iqbal, was a poet-philosopher of British India who wrote in Urdu and Persian. His poetry, including Shikwa and the philosophy of Khudi (selfhood), stirred a generation to self-respect and action. He is honoured as the national poet of Pakistan.

Jaun Elia.bio: Syed Sibt-e-Asghar Naqvi, known as Jaun Elia, was a Pakistani Urdu poet, scholar and philosopher born in Amroha, India. His verse blends deep classical learning with a rebellious, melancholic wit unlike any other Urdu poet. His first collection, Shayad, appeared in 1991, yet his couplets are among the most quoted in the language.

Mir Taqi Mir.bio: Mir Taqi Mir, honoured as Khuda-e-Sukhan (God of Poetry), was the pre-eminent Urdu poet of eighteenth-century Delhi and Lucknow. His ghazals of love, loss and the decline of Delhi set the standard for classical Urdu poetry. His six diwans and masnavis remain central to the Urdu canon.

Harivansh Rai Bachchan.bio: Harivansh Rai Bachchan was one of the most popular Hindi poets of the twentieth century, famed for Madhushala (1935) and the fiery poem Agneepath. He taught at Allahabad University and earned a doctorate from Cambridge on the poet W. B. Yeats. He was the father of actor Amitabh Bachchan.

Mahadevi Varma.bio: Mahadevi Varma was a leading poet of the Chhayavaad movement in Hindi literature and a pioneer of women's education in India. Her collections, including Rashmi and Neerja, weave mysticism, longing and compassion. She received the Jnanpith Award and the Padma Vibhushan.

Subhadra Kumari Chauhan.bio: Subhadra Kumari Chauhan was a Hindi poet celebrated for heroic ballads such as Jhansi ki Rani, which became an anthem of Indian nationalism. She was also a freedom fighter who took part in Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement. Her poems and stories for children remain beloved across India.

Ramdhari Singh Dinkar.bio: Ramdhari Singh Dinkar, honoured as Rashtrakavi (the national poet), was a Hindi poet of rebellion, nationalism and moral fire. His epics Kurukshetra and Rashmirathi retell the Mahabharata with bold questioning of war, fate and forgiveness. He received the Jnanpith Award and served in India's Rajya Sabha.

Javed Akhtar.bio: Javed Akhtar is an Indian poet, film lyricist and screenwriter who, with Salim Khan, wrote classics such as Sholay and Deewaar. His Urdu poetry collections Tarkash and Lava combine romance with sharp social conscience. He has won multiple National Film Awards and the Padma Bhushan.

Gulzar.bio: Gulzar, born Sampooran Singh Kalra, is an Indian poet, lyricist and filmmaker writing in Urdu and Hindi. His film songs, from Anand to the Oscar-winning 'Jai Ho', and his three-line Triveni poetry made him a household name. He has received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, the Sahitya Akademi Award and the Jnanpith.

Munshi Premchand.bio: Dhanpat Rai Srivastava, known as Munshi Premchand, was the most influential Hindi-Urdu fiction writer of his era. Novels such as Godaan and stories such as Kafan and Idgah portrayed the struggles of peasants, women and the poor with unmatched realism. He wrote around three hundred short stories and a dozen novels.

Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay.bio: Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay was Bengal's most widely read novelist, whose Devdas, Parineeta and Srikanta depict love, family and rural society. His works have been translated into many languages and adapted into numerous films. He is remembered for his deep compassion for women and the marginalised.

Bankim Chandra Chatterjee.bio: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee pioneered the Bengali novel with works such as Durgeshnandini, Kapalkundala and Anandamath. Anandamath gave India the hymn Vande Mataram, which became a rallying song of the freedom movement. He is regarded as the father of the modern Bengali novel.

Michael Madhusudan Dutt.bio: Michael Madhusudan Dutt introduced blank verse, the epic form and the sonnet into Bengali poetry. His masterpiece Meghnad Badh Kavya (1861) retells the Ramayana with the demon prince Meghnad as its tragic hero. Writing in both English and Bengali, he transformed the course of Bengali literature.

Kazi Nazrul Islam.bio: Kazi Nazrul Islam, the Bidrohi Kavi or Rebel Poet, was a Bengali poet, musician and revolutionary voice against colonial oppression. His poem Bidrohi and his songs of Hindu-Muslim unity made him a legend across Bengal. He is the national poet of Bangladesh.

George Washington.role: First President of the United States
George Washington.bio: George Washington commanded the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War and presided over the Constitutional Convention of 1787. He served as the first President of the United States from 1789 to 1797, setting enduring precedents for the office. He is remembered as the Father of His Country.

Julius Caesar.bio: Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman whose conquest of Gaul extended Rome's power to the Rhine and the English Channel. As dictator he reformed the calendar and the state before his assassination on the Ides of March, 44 BC. His commentaries on the Gallic Wars remain classics of Latin prose.

Cleopatra.bio: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, famed for her intellect, her command of many languages, and her alliances with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony. Defeated by Octavian after the Battle of Actium, she died in 30 BC as Egypt became a Roman province. Her life and words survive chiefly through the ancient historians Plutarch and Cassius Dio.

Queen Victoria.bio: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901, the longest reign of any British monarch until Elizabeth II. The Victorian era saw industrial growth, a vast empire and sweeping social change, and she became Empress of India in 1876. Her journals and letters fill volumes, and her devotion to Prince Albert shaped her life after his early death.

Elizabeth I.bio: The last Tudor monarch, Elizabeth I reigned over England from 1558 to 1603, an era of flourishing arts, exploration and naval triumph. Never married, she famously declared herself wedded to her kingdom and defended it against the Spanish Armada in 1588.

Catherine the Great.bio: Born a German princess, Catherine seized the Russian throne in 1762 and reigned for 34 years. An Enlightenment correspondent of Voltaire and Diderot, she expanded Russia's borders and modernised its administration, arts and culture.

Joan of Arc.bio: A peasant girl from Domremy, Joan said divine voices guided her to lift the siege of Orleans in 1429 and see Charles VII crowned at Reims. Captured, tried for heresy and burned at Rouen in 1431, she was canonised in 1920 and is a patron saint of France.

Marie Antoinette.bio: The Austrian-born queen consort of Louis XVI, Marie Antoinette became a symbol of royal excess during the French Revolution, though the infamous 'let them eat cake' line was never actually hers. She was guillotined in Paris in October 1793, months after her husband.

Rosa Parks.bio: A seamstress and NAACP activist in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks refused to surrender her bus seat to a white passenger on 1 December 1955. Her arrest sparked the 381-day Montgomery bus boycott and made her an enduring icon of the American civil rights movement.

Greta Thunberg.bio: Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg began a solo school strike outside Sweden's parliament in August 2018, aged fifteen. Her Fridays for Future protest grew into a global youth movement, and she has addressed the United Nations and the Davos forum demanding urgent action on the climate crisis.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Bill Gates.bio: Bill Gates co-founded Microsoft in 1975 and built the software that powered the personal computer revolution, leading the company for 25 years. He later devoted himself to philanthropy, co-founding the Gates Foundation, one of the world's largest charitable organisations.

Elon Musk.role: Entrepreneur, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX
Elon Musk.bio: South African-born entrepreneur Elon Musk co-founded PayPal before building Tesla into the world's leading electric carmaker and SpaceX into a pioneer of reusable rockets. Known for audacious goals, from colonising Mars to brain-computer interfaces, he is among the world's wealthiest people.

Jeff Bezos.bio: Jeff Bezos founded Amazon in 1994 as an online bookstore and grew it into one of the world's most valuable companies, reshaping retail and cloud computing along the way. He stepped down as CEO in 2021 and also founded the spaceflight company Blue Origin.

Warren Buffett.bio: Investor Warren Buffett, the 'Oracle of Omaha', turned Berkshire Hathaway into one of the world's largest conglomerates through patient, disciplined value investing. Famous for his annual shareholder letters and frugal personal habits, he has pledged to give away the great majority of his fortune.

Richard Branson.bio: British entrepreneur Richard Branson founded the Virgin brand with a mail-order record business in 1970 and expanded it into airlines, telecoms, hotels and space tourism. A flamboyant risk-taker, he has set world records in ballooning and flew to the edge of space aboard his own Virgin Galactic craft in 2021.

Andrew Carnegie.bio: Scottish-American steel magnate Andrew Carnegie built Carnegie Steel into the largest steel empire of the nineteenth century. After selling his company in 1901, he devoted his fortune to philanthropy, funding some 2,500 public libraries and preaching his 'Gospel of Wealth'.

John D. Rockefeller.bio: Co-founder of Standard Oil, John D. Rockefeller became America's first billionaire and is often regarded as the richest American of all time. In later life he turned to philanthropy, helping to found the University of Chicago and the Rockefeller Foundation.

Estee Lauder.bio: Estee Lauder founded her cosmetics company in 1946 with a handful of products and a genius for personal selling, elegant packaging and the free sample. She built it into a global beauty empire and was the only woman on Time magazine's 1998 list of the twenty most influential business figures of the century.

Sam Walton.bio: Sam Walton opened the first Walmart in Rogers, Arkansas, in 1962, preaching rock-bottom prices for small-town America. His relentless focus on costs, logistics and the customer built the world's largest retailer and made him, for a time, America's richest man.

Ratan Tata.role: Industrialist, chairman emeritus of Tata Sons
Ratan Tata.bio: Chairman of Tata Sons for more than two decades, Ratan Tata transformed the Tata group into a global conglomerate with acquisitions such as Tetley, Corus and Jaguar Land Rover. Revered in India for his integrity and philanthropy, he also championed the Tata Nano, the world's cheapest car.

Dhirubhai Ambani.bio: Dhirubhai Ambani rose from a petrol station attendant in Yemen to found Reliance, growing it from a small textile trading firm into India's largest private-sector conglomerate. He pioneered India's equity culture, drawing hundreds of thousands of small investors into the stock market.

Narayana Murthy.bio: N. R. Narayana Murthy co-founded Infosys in 1981 with six colleagues and a small borrowed sum, and led it into a global IT services giant. A champion of corporate governance and what he calls compassionate capitalism, he is widely regarded as the father of India's IT sector.

Azim Premji.bio: Azim Premji took over his family's cooking-oil business at twenty-one and diversified Wipro into a global IT services leader. One of India's most generous philanthropists, he was the first Indian to sign the Giving Pledge and has endowed the Azim Premji Foundation with most of his wealth.

Serena Williams.bio: American tennis legend who won 23 Grand Slam singles titles, the most in the Open Era, along with four Olympic gold medals. Born in Saginaw, Michigan, and raised in Compton, California, she dominated women's tennis for over two decades and became a successful businesswoman and advocate for women.

Sachin Tendulkar.bio: Indian cricket icon widely regarded as one of the greatest batsmen in history, scoring 100 international centuries across a 24-year career. He debuted for India at just 16 in 1989 and retired in 2013 after a record 200 Test matches, carrying the hopes of a billion fans.

Virat Kohli.bio: Indian batsman and former national captain, celebrated for his intense fitness, aggressive batting and record-breaking run chases in one-day internationals. He captained India to the 2008 Under-19 World Cup title as a teenager and became one of the most prolific run-scorers in modern cricket.

M. S. Dhoni.bio: Indian wicketkeeper-batsman and captain who led India to the 2007 T20 World Cup, the 2011 ODI World Cup and the 2013 Champions Trophy, the only captain to win all three ICC white-ball titles. Nicknamed 'Captain Cool', he is revered for his calm finishing of matches under pressure.

Pele.bio: Brazilian footballer widely considered the greatest player of all time, the only man to win three World Cups, in 1958, 1962 and 1970. He scored more than a thousand career goals for Santos and Brazil and was named FIFA's Player of the Century.

Diego Maradona.bio: Argentine football genius who captained his country to victory at the 1986 World Cup, scoring the famous 'Goal of the Century' against England. Brilliant and controversial in equal measure, he starred for Boca Juniors, Barcelona and Napoli, where he remains a folk hero.

Lionel Messi.bio: Argentine forward regarded as one of the greatest footballers ever, winner of a record eight Ballon d'Or awards. After 21 years at Barcelona he moved to Paris Saint-Germain and then Inter Miami, and in 2022 he captained Argentina to the World Cup title.

Cristiano Ronaldo.bio: Portuguese forward and five-time Ballon d'Or winner, the all-time top scorer in men's international football and in the UEFA Champions League. Born in Madeira, he starred for Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus before moving to Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

Usain Bolt.bio: Jamaican sprinter, the fastest man in history, who set world records in the 100 metres (9.58 seconds) and 200 metres (19.19 seconds) in 2009. He won eight Olympic gold medals across the 2008, 2012 and 2016 Games and became famous for his 'lightning bolt' celebration pose.

Michael Phelps.bio: American swimmer and the most decorated Olympian of all time, with 28 Olympic medals, 23 of them gold. He won a record eight golds at the 2008 Beijing Games and has since become a prominent advocate for mental health awareness.

Jackie Chan.bio: Hong Kong actor, martial artist and stunt performer famous for performing his own dangerous stunts and blending action with physical comedy. Trained at a Peking opera school from childhood, he rose to stardom with Drunken Master and Rush Hour and received an honorary Academy Award in 2016.

Arnold Schwarzenegger.bio: Austrian-born bodybuilder who won seven Mr. Olympia titles before becoming one of Hollywood's biggest action stars with films such as The Terminator and Total Recall. He later served two terms as Governor of California, from 2003 to 2011.

Dwayne Johnson.bio: American actor and former professional wrestler known as 'The Rock', one of WWE's biggest stars before moving into Hollywood. He became one of the world's highest-paid actors through the Fast & Furious and Jumanji franchises and co-founded Seven Bucks Productions.

Tom Cruise.bio: American actor and producer, one of Hollywood's most enduring stars for over four decades and famous for performing his own stunts in the Mission: Impossible series. His hits range from Top Gun and Jerry Maguire to Top Gun: Maverick, one of the highest-grossing films of all time.

Shah Rukh Khan.bio: Indian actor known as the 'King of Bollywood', one of the world's most popular film stars with a career spanning more than a hundred films. Rising from television in the late 1980s, he became a global icon with films like Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge and co-owns the Kolkata Knight Riders cricket team.

Amitabh Bachchan.bio: Legendary Indian actor, the defining superstar of Hindi cinema since the 1970s with classics such as Zanjeer, Deewaar and Sholay. After a celebrated career revival in the 2000s, he has hosted the quiz show Kaun Banega Crorepati for over two decades and remains Bollywood's most revered figure.

Rajinikanth.bio: Superstar of Tamil cinema, worshipped by fans for his inimitable style, screen presence and dialogue delivery. Born Shivaji Rao Gaekwad, he worked as a bus conductor in Bangalore before debuting in 1975, and went on to become one of Asia's highest-paid actors.

Aamir Khan.bio: Indian actor and filmmaker known as Bollywood's 'Mr. Perfectionist' for his meticulous and highly selective choice of roles. His films, including Lagaan, 3 Idiots and Dangal, rank among the highest-grossing Indian films ever and often blend entertainment with social themes.

Leonardo DiCaprio.bio: American actor who rose from child roles to global stardom with Titanic and won the Academy Award for Best Actor for The Revenant in 2016. Off screen he is a leading environmental activist and founded the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation in 1998 to protect wildlife and fight climate change.

Marilyn Monroe.bio: American actress and the most enduring sex symbol of Hollywood's golden age, starring in comedies such as Gentlemen Prefer Blondes and Some Like It Hot. Born Norma Jeane Mortenson, she fought to be taken seriously as an actress and founded her own production company in 1955.

Audrey Hepburn.bio: Audrey Hepburn was a British actress and humanitarian celebrated for films such as Roman Holiday, Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady. In later life she devoted herself to UNICEF, serving as a Goodwill Ambassador in some of the world's poorest regions.

Charlie Chaplin.bio: Charlie Chaplin was an English comic actor and filmmaker whose Little Tramp became a global icon of silent cinema. He co-founded United Artists and wrote, directed and starred in classics including City Lights, Modern Times and The Great Dictator.

David Hume.bio: David Hume was a Scottish Enlightenment philosopher, historian and economist, best known for A Treatise of Human Nature and An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding. His scepticism about causation, miracles and the self profoundly influenced Western philosophy.

Archimedes.bio: Archimedes of Syracuse was a Greek mathematician, physicist and inventor regarded as one of the greatest mathematicians of antiquity. He calculated an accurate approximation of pi, formulated the principle of buoyancy, and designed machines such as the screw pump and compound pulleys.

Euclid.bio: Euclid was a Greek mathematician active in Alexandria around 300 BCE, often called the father of geometry. His Elements, a systematic treatment of geometry and number theory in thirteen books, remained the standard mathematical textbook for more than two thousand years.

Aryabhata.bio: Aryabhata was an Indian mathematician and astronomer whose Aryabhatiya, composed in 499 CE, gave an accurate approximation of pi and described the rotation of the Earth on its axis. He advanced the use of place value in Indian mathematics and correctly explained the causes of eclipses.

C. V. Raman.bio: Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman was an Indian physicist who won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering that light changes wavelength when it passes through a transparent material, the Raman effect. He founded the Indian Academy of Sciences and the Raman Research Institute in Bengaluru.

Satyendra Nath Bose.bio: Satyendra Nath Bose was an Indian physicist whose 1924 work on quantum statistics, developed with Albert Einstein, predicted a new state of matter, the Bose-Einstein condensate. The class of particles known as bosons is named after him.

Homi Bhabha.bio: Homi Jehangir Bhabha was an Indian nuclear physicist who founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and chaired the Atomic Energy Commission. Regarded as the father of India's nuclear programme, he built it around a three-stage plan based on India's thorium reserves.

Vikram Sarabhai.bio: Vikram Sarabhai was an Indian physicist and innovator who founded the Indian Space Research Organisation and the Physical Research Laboratory. Known as the father of the Indian space programme, he insisted that advanced technology be applied to the real problems of man and society.

Verghese Kurien.bio: Verghese Kurien was an Indian social entrepreneur who built the Anand cooperative model behind Amul and led Operation Flood, the world's largest dairy development programme. His work turned India from a milk-deficient nation into the world's largest milk producer, lifting millions of farmers out of poverty.

M. Visvesvaraya.bio: Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya was an Indian civil engineer who designed the Krishna Raja Sagara dam and served as Diwan of Mysore from 1912 to 1918. A pioneer of planned industrialisation whose slogan was 'Industrialize or perish', he founded institutions including the Mysore Soap Factory and the State Bank of Mysore.

Jagadish Chandra Bose.bio: Jagadish Chandra Bose was an Indian physicist and plant physiologist who pioneered the investigation of radio and microwave optics and demonstrated that plants respond to stimuli. He founded the Bose Institute in Calcutta in 1917 and is considered a father of radio science.

Srinivasa Ramanujan.bio: Srinivasa Ramanujan was a largely self-taught Indian mathematician who, working with G. H. Hardy at Cambridge, produced some 3,900 results in number theory, infinite series and continued fractions. His intuitive genius and early death at 32 made him one of mathematics' most celebrated figures.

Kalpana Chawla.bio: Kalpana Chawla was an Indian-American astronaut and engineer, the first woman of Indian origin to fly in space. She flew on two Space Shuttle Columbia missions and died in the Columbia disaster of 1 February 2003, along with her six crewmates.

Sunita Williams.bio: Sunita Williams is an American astronaut and retired US Navy officer of Indian-Slovenian heritage who has flown multiple long-duration missions to the International Space Station. She has commanded the ISS and set records for spacewalking by a woman.

Rakesh Sharma.bio: Rakesh Sharma is a former Indian Air Force pilot who, on 3 April 1984, became the first Indian citizen to travel to space, flying aboard the Soviet Soyuz T-11 to the Salyut 7 station. Asked by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi how India looked from space, he famously replied, 'Saare Jahan Se Achha.'
